passage: Helmets? I rode my bike to the plant every day for twenty-two years without one and never so much as scraped my head. I'm not against them, but all those head-injury studies get blown way out of proportion. Anyway, who wants another burger?
cue: twenty-two years without one and never so much as scraped my head
explanation: Ray uses his own lucky record to wave away research on head injuries. One rider avoiding a bad crash says little about what happens across thousands of crashes.

whyNot.fal_hasty_generalization: Ray isn't building a rule from a few cases so much as using his single story to outweigh the studies he mentions.

title: Ignore the ratings, this car is bulletproof
passage: Every reliability survey out there puts the Vantessa sedan near the bottom of its class, and I honestly don't get it. Mine has 140,000 miles and has never needed anything but oil changes and tires. Comfortable seats, decent mileage, roomy trunk. Don't let the ratings scare you off: this car is built to last.
cue: Mine has 140,000 miles and has never needed anything but oil changes and tires.
explanation: Tom lets his one good car outweigh surveys of thousands of owners. Some Vantessas will run perfectly even if the model breaks down more often than its rivals, so his story can't overturn the ratings.

whyNot.fal_cherry_picking: Tom isn't picking favorable numbers out of a dataset; he's setting a single personal story against the surveys.

passage: Every article says adults need 7-9 hours of sleep. I've slept about five hours a night for a decade, I run marathons and I manage a team of twelve. To be fair, people really do differ, and that research describes averages. But in my experience, you can train your body to need less, so stop stressing about the eight-hour rule.
cue: in my experience, you can train your body to need less
explanation: Kara sets her own routine against broad sleep research and concludes anyone can train themselves to need less. Her experience can be real without telling others what's safe for them.

whyNot.fal_hasty_generalization: Kara explicitly weighs her story against the research and lets it win; that's anecdote over data, not just a small sample.

title: Re: Remote connection program
passage: Thanks for sharing the engagement results. I know the survey of 430 staff found remote employees feel less connected, and I'm not dismissing it. But my remote team is the closest group I've ever managed; we do video coffee every Friday and nobody's quit in two years. Honestly, I don't think the connection program is needed.
cue: my remote team is the closest group I've ever managed
explanation: Victor's team may be genuinely close, but he uses it to set aside a survey of 430 people. One team's experience can't outweigh what the broader data shows across the company.

whyNot.fal_cherry_picking: Victor isn't selecting data points from the survey; he's countering the whole survey with his own team's story.

passage:
Ji-woo: The district report is out: across three years, kids in the ReadUp program gained about 1.5 grade levels on average.
Maria: That's encouraging!
Ji-woo: Maybe. Daniel did a full year of it and his reading didn't budge. Honestly, I'm not convinced it does much, and I'd rather the PTA funded something else.
cue: Daniel did a full year of it and his reading didn't budge
explanation: Ji-woo's frustration is understandable, but she lets her son's year outweigh three years of district-wide results. An average gain still leaves room for some kids who don't improve.

whyNot.fal_hasty_generalization: Ji-woo isn't building a claim from a few cases; she has the district data in front of her and lets one child's story overrule it.

source: Resident Glen Harlow · Pine County water board hearing
passage: I've read the county's report saying nitrate levels in rural wells along Route 6 have climbed past the safety limit. With respect, my family has drunk from our well for thirty years. Three kids, six grandkids, all healthy as horses. I don't doubt the lab did its job, but I don't see why we need to spend money on filters.
cue: my family has drunk from our well for thirty years
explanation: Glen's family history feels like strong evidence, but it can't outweigh lab tests of the water itself. Thirty healthy years don't show today's water is safe, especially since the levels have recently climbed.

whyNot.fal_hasty_generalization: Glen isn't sampling a few wells; he sets his family's experience against the county's tests and lets the story win.

passage: Two weeks with the Corvel 14 laptop. On normal workdays (browser, docs, video calls) I'm getting about nine hours per charge. That lines up with the 9.5 hours the Benchline Labs team measured in its standardized test, so I'm fairly convinced the 'all-day battery' claim holds up for office work. Gaming, I'd guess, is a different story.
cue: That lines up with the 9.5 hours the Benchline Labs team measured
explanation: Hana shares her own experience but checks it against a standardized lab test, and she limits her conclusion to office work. Her story supports the data instead of replacing it.

whyNot.fal_anecdotal_evidence: Hana's experience agrees with systematic testing and she claims only what both support, so her story isn't outweighing the evidence.

title: Does NOT fit every phone
passage: The listing says this car mount 'fits every phone.' Mine measures 3.4 inches across in a slim case, and it won't fit no matter how I adjust it. The included manual lists the clamp's maximum opening as 3.2 inches. So whatever else is true, 'every phone' is simply wrong. It's sturdy and holds my partner's smaller phone well, hence two stars.
cue: The included manual lists the clamp's maximum opening as 3.2 inches
explanation: Noor uses her experience only to test an 'every phone' claim, and the manual's own specs confirm it. A single real counterexample is enough to show an absolute claim is false.

whyNot.fal_anecdotal_evidence: Noor isn't setting a story against broad data; one confirmed counterexample is exactly what it takes to refute an 'every' claim.
